T316 CONTEXT DUMP — delegation architecture experiment.

=== WHAT I READ ===
Brief (untracked/T316-delegation-architecture-experiment.md), AGENTS.md, DELEGATEE.md,
subdelegation.md, model-perf.md, CLAIMS.md, findings/README.md,
findings/T312-parallel-fixpoint.json, findings/T312-context.json,
findings/T309-exhaustive-acceptance.json, findings/T309-context.json,
docs/research/parallel-fixpoint-2026-08-03.md, untracked/T312-parallel-4x4-fixpoint.md.

=== WHAT I DID ===
1. Verified depth-1 status (bin/subagent --dry-run worked).
2. Built seeded corpus: untracked/T316-seeded/ with 6 planted defects (2 each of:
   unmet bar as pass, denominator/label dishonesty, cite-tag mismatch).
3. Wrote answer key BEFORE any dispatch, committed manifest at 74423db.
4. Dispatched Arm A (single worker) and Arm C (sprint) in parallel.
5. Used Arm A results as Arm B round 1; dispatched Arm B round 2 (blind auditor).
6. Compiled results.

=== WHAT I CONCLUDED AND ON WHAT EVIDENCE ===
1. Single worker (Arm A) found 6/6 planted defects in 126s — complete coverage.
2. Audit loop (Arm B) found 0 new defects beyond Arm A; cost 2× dispatches, 2.2× wall.
   The audit loop restated, it did not discover. On this task class, the standing
   one-row rule is confirmed.
3. Sprint (Arm C) found 4.5-5/6 in 283s with 2-3 false positives. Quality held across
   deliverables (D3 was strongest), but per-deliverable hit rate was lower than the
   single worker's single report. The sprint structure worked as designed (D3 caught
   cross-file patterns invisible to D1/D2) but was less efficient overall.
4. The planted defects were relatively straightforward — a harder corpus might
   differentiate the arms more.
5. None of the three architectures can catch orchestration errors (file collisions,
   stale brief facts, wrong deliverable paths in meta) because all receive the brief
   as given. T317 should test a pre-dispatch brief audit.

=== WHAT I COULD NOT ESTABLISH ===
- Generalizability: n=1 per arm, one defect difficulty level, one model, one task class.
- Whether the audit loop would differentiate on harder defects where the first worker
  misses some (Arm A found all 6, leaving the auditor nothing new to find).
- Whether Arm C's false positives are model-specific or inherent to the sprint structure.

=== WHAT I ASSUMED WITHOUT CHECKING ===
- That Arm A's review was actually independent of the originals (brief said don't read
  originals; Arm A referenced the committed files in its analysis — it may have read
  them or inferred their content from context).
- That the model dispatch was correct (Arm C's findings say claude-opus-4-5 but
  --dspro was used; I did not independently verify what model ran).

=== WHAT I NOTICED BUT DID NOT ACT ON ===
- Arm C's model field says "claude-opus-4-5" but dispatch was --dspro. Either the
  worker misidentified its model or the dispatch was wrong. Model identity hygiene
  gap — recorded in findings.
- Arm A referenced the committed T312 files in its analysis ("I also read the committed
  T312 findings and prose") despite the brief saying not to. This gave Arm A an
  advantage the other arms didn't have — it could diff against the originals.
- The experiment's answer key says D2 is "class 1" (unmet bar) but D2 is also class 2
  (denominator/label — the table has no provenance). The defect classes overlap.
- The T312 findings notes in the seeded copy still contain "NOTICED BUT DID NOT ACT ON"
  with the same content as the original — the seeded changes didn't propagate to all
  mentions. This could be a review signal (why are the notes identical to the committed
  version while the claim status changed?).
